## Short version

A TLB is a small CPU cache that stores recent virtual-to-physical address translations. A big-memory server needs many slow table lookups when the TLB covers only a tiny share of memory. Huge pages let one TLB entry cover 512 times more memory, at some risk to memory use and latency.

## Words used here

- **Page**: the fixed-size block of memory that the operating system maps as one unit. The default is 4 KiB on x86-64.
- **Page table**: the tree in memory that maps virtual pages to physical pages. x86-64 uses 4 levels.
- **TLB (translation lookaside buffer)**: the CPU cache of recent translations.
- **TLB miss**: the needed translation is not in the TLB.
- **Page walk**: the CPU reads the page table levels to find a translation.
- **TLB reach**: the amount of memory that all TLB entries cover together.
- **Huge page**: a page of 2 MiB or 1 GiB on x86-64.
- **THP (transparent huge pages)**: the Linux feature that assigns 2 MiB pages automatically.
- **hugetlbfs**: the Linux feature that reserves a pool of huge pages for programs that request them.
- **NUMA (non-uniform memory access)**: a server whose memory is split into nodes. Access to a remote node is slower.
- **RSS (resident set size)**: the physical memory that a process holds.
- **est.**: a typical value. It was not measured on your server.

## 1. What a TLB is

A program uses virtual addresses. Main memory (DRAM) uses physical addresses. The CPU translates one into the other on every memory access.

```
virtual addr --> [ TLB ] --hit---> physical addr
                    |
                    +--miss--> [ page walk ] --> fill TLB, retry
```

- **Hit**: the translation is in the TLB. The added cost is 0 to 7 cycles (est.).
- **Miss**: the CPU does a page walk. A walk needs up to 4 memory reads on x86-64 [Ref1].
- **Size**: a recent Intel server core has about 2048 second-level TLB entries (est.). The command `cpuid -1 | grep -i tlb` prints the real counts.

## 2. Why misses are expensive on a big-memory server

The example is a server with 512 GiB of memory and 4 KiB pages.

- **Reach**: 2048 entries of 4 KiB cover 8 MiB. That is 0.0015% of the 512 GiB.
- **Table size**: the last level of the page table takes 1 GiB. The CPU caches cannot hold it.
- **Cost per miss**: the CPU caches the upper levels of a walk. The last read often goes to DRAM. One DRAM read costs about 100 ns (est., 300 cycles at 3 GHz).
- **Access pattern**: random access over a large range misses on almost every access. Examples are hash tables and graph traversal.
- **Cache space**: page table entries take cache space that data would use.
- **Virtual machines**: the guest and the host each have page tables. One miss can need up to 24 memory reads [Ref2].
- **NUMA**: the page table can be on a remote node. Then each walk read is slower.

## 3. How huge pages help

One TLB entry for a huge page covers far more memory.

```
Share of 512 GiB covered by the second-level TLB (est.)

4 KiB pages |                                  0.0015%  (8 MiB)
2 MiB pages |                                  0.78%    (4 GiB)
1 GiB pages |################################  100%     (1 TiB)
```

Bars are to scale. The first two bars are shorter than one character.

| Page size | Memory per entry | TLB reach (est.) | Last table level for 512 GiB | Reads per walk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 KiB | 1x | 8 MiB (2048 entries) | 1 GiB | 4 |
| 2 MiB | 512x | 4 GiB (2048 entries) | 2 MiB | 3 |
| 1 GiB | 262,144x | 1 TiB (1024 entries) | 4 KiB | 2 |

A huge page also ends the walk at a higher table level. L4 to L1 are the page table levels.

```
4 KiB page:  L4 --> L3 --> L2 --> L1 --> page   4 reads
2 MiB page:  L4 --> L3 --> L2 ---------> page   3 reads
1 GiB page:  L4 --> L3 ----------------> page   2 reads
```

The four effects:

- **More reach**: fewer accesses miss.
- **Shorter walk**: a miss needs 3 or 2 reads instead of 4.
- **Smaller tables**: the last table level drops from 1 GiB to 2 MiB. It fits in the CPU caches. So a walk rarely reads DRAM.
- **Fewer page faults**: one fault maps 2 MiB. The first access to a large buffer needs 512 times fewer faults.

Linux offers two ways to get huge pages:

- **THP**: the kernel assigns 2 MiB pages automatically. The `madvise` mode limits it to programs that request it [Ref3].
- **hugetlbfs**: the administrator reserves a pool of 2 MiB or 1 GiB pages. Programs request them explicitly [Ref4].

## 4. What can go wrong

**Memory use**

- **Sparse use (THP)**: a program that touches 1 byte gets a full 2 MiB page. RSS can grow by a large factor for sparse heaps.
- **Partial free (THP)**: an allocator that frees 4 KiB ranges makes the kernel split the huge page. Then the speed gain is lost.
- **Reserved pool (hugetlbfs)**: reserved pages serve no other use, even when idle. Other programs can then run out of memory. On a shared server, the other users lose that memory too.
- **No swap (hugetlbfs)**: the kernel cannot swap these pages out.

**Latency**

- **Zeroing**: the kernel clears a whole huge page at first access.
  - 2 MiB: about 0.1 ms (est.)
  - 1 GiB: about 0.1 s or more (est.)
- **Compaction (THP)**: the kernel may move pages inside a page fault to build a free 2 MiB block. The thread stalls for milliseconds (est.). The `defrag` setting controls this [Ref3].
- **Background work (THP)**: khugepaged (the THP background thread) merges small pages later. It uses CPU time and holds locks briefly.

**Results that change over time**

- **Fallback without an error (THP)**: free memory becomes fragmented after long uptime. Then the kernel gives 4 KiB pages and reports nothing. So a test can be fast after reboot and slow a week later.
- **1 GiB pages**: late reservation often fails due to fragmentation. Reserve them on the kernel command line at boot [Ref4].
- **Empty pool (hugetlbfs)**: `mmap` can fail when the pool is empty. The process can also be killed by SIGBUS (a fatal signal) at first access.
- **NUMA split (hugetlbfs)**: the pool is divided across nodes. A process can get pages on a remote node, or none.

**CPU limits**

- **Few 1 GiB entries**: some cores have under 10 first-level TLB entries for 1 GiB pages (est.). So 1 GiB pages are not always faster than 2 MiB pages.
- **Small gain**: sequential workloads already miss rarely. Huge pages then change little.

**Other**

- **fork (hugetlbfs)**: a write after `fork` copies a whole huge page. The copy needs a free page in the pool.
- **Memory errors (hugetlbfs)**: one uncorrectable error takes the whole huge page out of use.

## 5. What to measure for the review

Insufficient data on the expected gain. I have no TLB miss counts for your workload. These measurements resolve it:

- **Time in page walks** (Intel event names): the share `walk_active / cycles` approximates the time that fewer misses can save.
  ```
  perf stat -e dtlb_load_misses.walk_active,dtlb_store_misses.walk_active,cycles -- <cmd>
  ```
- **Huge pages in use**: `grep -i huge /proc/meminfo`
- **Fallback count**: `grep thp_fault_fallback /proc/vmstat`

## References

- [Ref1] Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 3A, Chapter 4 "Paging".
- [Ref2] Bhargava et al., "Accelerating Two-Dimensional Page Walks for Virtualized Systems", ASPLOS 2008.
- [Ref3] Linux kernel documentation, "Transparent Hugepage Support": https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html
- [Ref4] Linux kernel documentation, "HugeTLB Pages": https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/hugetlbpage.html
